---
title: "S3 paths and credentials"
---

[Universal Pathlib](https://universal-pathlib.readthedocs.io/) makes S3 objects as easy to
handle as local files, but Rasterio cannot use the configuration of its paths. An `s3://`
`UPath` supports `/`, `.exists()`, `.glob()` and `.open()` like a `pathlib.Path`, and carries
its credentials and endpoint in its `storage_options`.
[Rasterio](https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/) can open the same `s3://` URI through GDAL, but
GDAL takes credentials and endpoint from its own configuration and ignores those of the
`UPath`. Without a bridge, raster I/O on S3 needs the same configuration set up twice.

freezebase provides that bridge. `make_s3_upath()` builds an S3 `UPath`, and the raster
helpers, such as `rasterio_open()`, pass the path's configuration on to GDAL. One path then
serves file operations and raster I/O alike, and two paths in one process can point at
different accounts or at S3-compatible stores such as MinIO or Ceph:

```python
from freezebase.raster import rasterio_open
from freezebase.s3 import make_s3_upath

# The named profile travels with this path and all paths derived from it.
path = make_s3_upath("s3://my-bucket/scene.tif", profile="research")
if path.exists():
    with rasterio_open(path) as src:
        data = src.read(1)
```

This page shows how to build such paths. [Reading and writing rasters](03-rasters.qmd) covers
the raster helpers.

::: {.callout-note}
## Install the S3 extra

S3 support needs s3fs, fsspec, boto3 and pydantic-settings (the last for
`freezebase.settings`):

```bash
pip install "freezebase[s3]"
```

These are imported lazily, so local raster operations work with the base installation.
:::

## Choosing credentials

Each path uses one of four credential sources: a named profile, explicit keys, anonymous
access or boto's default credential chain.

### A named profile

If your credentials are stored as a profile in the AWS configuration files, pass the
profile's name. This is the recommended approach: the credentials stay in those files, out of
your code and environment variables, and the path stores only the name.

```ini
# ~/.aws/credentials
[research]
aws_access_key_id = ...
aws_secret_access_key = ...
```

```python
aws_path = make_s3_upath("s3://aws-bucket/data", profile="research")
```

Paths derived from `aws_path` inherit the profile, and s3fs and Rasterio each load it when they
access the store.

A profile can also set the endpoint of an S3-compatible store, so the code needs no URL:

```ini
# ~/.aws/config
[profile ceph-research]
region = eu-central-1
endpoint_url = https://objects.example.org
```

```python
ceph_path = make_s3_upath("s3://ceph-bucket/data", profile="ceph-research")
```

An `endpoint_url` argument overrides the endpoint from the configuration:

```python
ceph_path = make_s3_upath(
    "s3://ceph-bucket/data",
    profile="ceph-research",
    endpoint_url="https://objects.example.org",
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A profiled path ignores credentials in the environment

A path with a profile is never signed with an `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` or `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
set in the shell, because boto skips its environment-variable credential provider once a
profile is selected. Credentials meant for one service are therefore not sent to another.
:::

### Explicit keys

Explicit keys suit credentials that come from an application's own secret store rather than
an AWS configuration file:

```python
custom = make_s3_upath(
    "s3://imagery/scene.tif",
    key=...,
    secret=...,
    token=...,  # optional STS/session token
    endpoint_url="https://objects.example.org",
    region="eu-central-1",
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Treat these paths as sensitive

Explicit `key`, `secret` and `token` values are stored in the `UPath`'s `storage_options`. Do
not log, publish or serialize those options. A named profile keeps the credential values off
the path.
:::

### Anonymous access

Public buckets need anonymous access, which has to be requested explicitly:

```python
public = make_s3_upath("s3://public-bucket/scene.tif", anon=True)
```

### The default credential chain

Without a profile, keys or `anon=True`, both s3fs and GDAL use boto's default credential
chain. This picks up environment variables and workload roles, but the identity a path uses
is no longer visible on the path.

## Settings from environment variables

`S3Settings` reads a profile, an endpoint and checksum policies from environment variables
under a prefix you choose. Its `resolve_path()` turns a local location into a `Path` and an
`s3://` URI into a `UPath`:

```python
from freezebase.settings import S3Settings

# Reads MYAPP_S3_PROFILE, MYAPP_S3_ENDPOINT_URL, and the two
# MYAPP_S3_*_CHECKSUM_* policies for S3-compatible gateways.
s3 = S3Settings.from_env("MYAPP_S3_")
data_dir = s3.resolve_path("s3://my-bucket/data")  # a UPath
scratch = s3.resolve_path("~/scratch")  # a Path
```

An `s3://` URI needs a configured profile. The endpoint is optional, since it can come from
the profile's configuration.

## Long-running processes

freezebase caches Rasterio sessions and configured endpoints, so a configuration change
during a process needs `clear_aws_session_cache()`. Resolving them means reading the AWS
configuration files, so sessions are cached by their credential settings and endpoints by
profile, and later reads and writes reuse them. Refreshable credentials, such as STS or SSO
profiles, still rotate on their own. After changing static credentials, the AWS config files
or the endpoint environment variables while a process runs, call `clear_aws_session_cache()`
so the next access resolves them again.

## Retries and checksums

`make_s3_upath()` also sets retries for both s3fs and GDAL, and checksum defaults that avoid
the checksum trailers some S3-compatible gateways reject.
